summary: R Draconis is a known red giant star of the Mira type. It swells and shrinks, so its brightness rises and falls over about 245 days. Gaia puts it about 2,607 light-years away. WANDERERS saw it fade by 0.32 ± 0.07 magnitudes from June to November 2025. Its center is too bright for SPHEREx, so we measured only the outer glow of its image. All 150 SPHEREx points are flagged, so we show no spectrum. We found no real motion. Gaia also lists it as this kind of variable star, so our confidence is high.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Two independent checks agree. Gaia DR3 matches this star and, from about three years of its own photometry, classifies it as a long-period Mira-type variable. SPHEREx saw it fade by 0.32 ± 0.07 magnitudes between June and November 2025. That change is over four times its uncertainty. But the star is too bright for SPHEREx: all 150 points are flagged, so we measured only the edges of its saturated image.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: The weak spot is brightness: R Draconis is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 150 measurements are flagged. The 0.32 ± 0.07 magnitude fade comes only from the wings of its saturated image. I would be less sure if wing measurements proved biased, or if Gaia did not also call it a long-period variable. The tiny apparent drift is below the detection limit, so it is not real motion.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE took images of this sky in 2010, and SPHEREx took them in 2025 and 2026. Together they give a 16-year baseline to test for motion. The apparent drift of 0.09 arcseconds per year is below the detection limit, so it is not real motion. SPHEREx adds many wavelengths and repeat visits. These showed a fade of 0.32 ± 0.07 mag, but the star saturates SPHEREx and all 150 spectrum points are flagged.
